topic: Irritable bowel syndrome and chronic diarrhoea
page_contents_html:
Irritable bowel syndrome and chronic diarrhoea

Use this pathway for adults with persistent loose stool or suspected IBS. Exclude cancer, inflammation, infection, coeliac disease, medicine effects and malabsorption, then make a positive diagnosis of IBS where appropriate.

Key testing messages

  • Include HIV serology in the initial GP investigation of chronic diarrhoea.
  • Do not request faecal calprotectin routinely for possible IBS. Use it for persistent loose stool when qFIT is negative and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History and examination

  • Clarify duration, stool frequency and form, abdominal pain, bloating, urgency, incontinence, blood or mucus, nocturnal symptoms and weight change.
  • Ask about recent antibiotics, travel or infection exposure; diet and alcohol; previous bowel or gallbladder surgery, pancreatitis or radiotherapy.
  • Review medicines that can cause diarrhoea, including laxatives, metformin, PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs and magnesium-containing products.
  • Ask about colorectal or ovarian cancer, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease in the family.

Assess hydration and nutrition. Examine the abdomen for tenderness or a mass and for faecal impaction or overflow. Perform rectal examination where clinically indicated.

Rome IV criteria

Make a positive diagnosis of IBS when there is recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with at least 2 of:

  • Related to defaecation
  • A change in stool frequency
  • A change in stool form

Symptoms should have started at least 6 months before diagnosis. Bloating, urgency, mucus and incomplete evacuation may support the diagnosis.

Initial investigations

Bloods: FBC, CRP (or ESR/plasma viscosity), coeliac serology with total IgA and TFT. Add renal and liver function, ferritin/iron studies and other tests according to the presentation. Include HIV serology for chronic diarrhoea.

Stool infection tests: request when infection is plausible; include ova, cysts and parasites when exposure or travel history is relevant.

When to request qFIT

Request qFIT for:

  • Repeated anorectal bleeding without an obvious anal cause, or blood mixed through the stool
  • Change in bowel habit for 4 weeks or more, particularly looser or more frequent stool
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia: haemoglobin below the reference range with ferritin <30 micrograms/L or confirmed on iron studies
  • Persistent abdominal pain for 4 weeks or more with weight loss of at least 5% or strong clinical suspicion

Do not wait for qFIT where there is an unexplained abdominal or anorectal mass or unexplained anal ulceration.

When to request faecal calprotectin

Request only when loose stool persists, qFIT is negative, colorectal cancer and infection have been considered, and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential. Do not use it for clear IBS-C, stable established IBS or as a cancer test. Interpret using the current NHS Dumfries & Galloway laboratory comment and local action thresholds.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Treat dehydration, significant nutritional or electrolyte disturbance, infection and other identified causes. Stop or adjust a possible causative medicine where safe and review the response.

IBS management

Explain the positive diagnosis, agree the main symptom to target and arrange review. Signpost to NHS Inform: IBS.

  • Diet and lifestyle: regular meals, adequate fluid, regular activity, and reduced excess caffeine, alcohol and fizzy drinks. Prefer soluble fibre such as oats or ispaghula to bran. A low-FODMAP or other exclusion diet should be supervised by a clinician with dietary expertise.
  • Pain or bloating: consider an antispasmodic as required.
  • IBS-D: loperamide is first choice; titrate towards a soft, formed stool.
  • IBS-C: consider a laxative, avoiding lactulose where possible. Consider linaclotide only after optimal or maximum tolerated previous laxatives have failed and constipation has been present for at least 12 months; review after 3 months.
  • Persistent pain: if laxatives, loperamide or antispasmodics have not helped, consider a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant. Start at the equivalent of amitriptyline 5-10 mg at night, usually not exceeding 30 mg. This is off-label: discuss and document informed consent. Review after 4 weeks and then every 6-12 months.

Consider cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or psychological therapy when symptoms remain refractory after 12 months of appropriate treatment.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer and how urgently
accordion_sections.html:
Emergency / same-day assessment

Arrange same-day assessment for severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance, haemodynamic compromise or significant ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding, suspected obstruction, peritonism or acute severe systemic illness.

Colorectal: Urgent Suspicion of Cancer (USC)

Refer to the colorectal service as USC for:

  • qFIT ≥20 micrograms Hb/g faeces with colorectal symptoms or iron-deficiency anaemia
  • Symptoms qualifying for qFIT when the person is unable or unwilling to complete the test
  • Unexplained abdominal mass
  • Palpable anorectal mass
  • Unexplained anal ulceration

Include the numerical qFIT result. Safety-net a test that is not returned. Iron-deficiency anaemia may still require investigation despite a normal qFIT.

Ovarian cancer assessment and USC referral

Palpate the abdomen, measure CA125 and arrange a USC pelvic ultrasound for:

  • Women, especially aged 50 or over, with unexplained abdominal distension or persistent bloating, early satiety/difficulty eating/loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency or change in bowel habit occurring most days over the last 4 weeks
  • Women aged 50 or over with new IBS-type symptoms within the last 12 months

Refer to gynaecology as USC for:

  • Ultrasound suggesting ovarian cancer or an abdominal/pelvic mass not clearly uterine, gastrointestinal or urological
  • CA125 ≥35 IU/mL
  • Unexplained ascites

If clinical concern is significant, do not delay referral while awaiting results.

Routine gastroenterology referral

  • Suspected inflammatory bowel disease, including a clearly raised or persistently borderline faecal calprotectin with compatible symptoms
  • Positive coeliac serology; advise the patient to continue eating gluten until assessment is complete
  • Persistent chronic diarrhoea with diagnostic uncertainty after the initial investigations
  • Evidence of malabsorption, pancreatic disease or another condition requiring specialist investigation
  • Severe or refractory IBS causing major functional impairment despite appropriate primary-care and specialist AHP input
  • The patient requests specialist review after an informed discussion

For chronic diarrhoea, include symptom pattern and duration, weight trend, medication review, examination, qFIT, faecal calprotectin if indicated, stool microbiology and blood results including HIV serology.

Dietetics / specialist AHP

Refer persistent IBS symptoms despite first-line advice for specialist dietary or other AHP input before medical gastroenterology where appropriate.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Manage in primary care when Rome IV criteria are met, there are no cancer or inflammatory features, initial investigations are satisfactory and symptoms are stable or improving with explanation, dietary measures or first-line medication.

Specialist referral is also unnecessary when a reversible medicine, dietary or short-lived infective cause has been identified and symptoms settle.

Do not arrange routine colonoscopy, ultrasound, breath testing, repeated inflammatory markers or repeated faecal calprotectin solely to reassure someone with a secure positive diagnosis of IBS.

notes_for_editor: This v2 replaces eight clinical accordions with the requested sequence: Primary care assessment, Primary care management, Who to refer and how urgently, and Who not to refer, followed by references.
Lower GI and ovarian assessment and USC thresholds are reproduced directly from the Scottish Referral Guidelines for Suspected Cancer 2025 rather than linked out as unspecified red flags.
Numerical faecal calprotectin thresholds remain omitted pending confirmation of the current D&G laboratory interpretive ranges.
